overview: This Annam card follows the colonial-era Nguyễn court and central Vietnamese society during the atlas’s 1920 to 1938 interval. The map is broader than the historical Annam protectorate: it includes Tonkin in the north and extends west of today’s Vietnamese frontier. Annam, Tonkin and Cochin China had different colonial administrations. These dates mark map coverage, not the beginning or end of French rule, and the examples below identify their local settings.

periods.title: Late Khải Định and royal succession
periods.summary: French control constrained the court. Khải Định died in November 1925; Bảo Đại was enthroned in January 1926.

periods.title: A young emperor abroad
periods.summary: Bảo Đại continued his education in France while a regency and the protectorate governed.

periods.title: Royal reforms under colonial limits
periods.summary: Bảo Đại returned and reorganized court government in 1933; French domination continued.

items.text: The treaties of 1883 and 1884 imposed French protection on the Nguyễn state. By the time of this map, the name Annam referred to the central protectorate, while Tonkin was a separate northern protectorate and Cochin China a southern colony. French authorities dominated the royal government, but Vietnamese officials still performed administrative work. A palace and an emperor therefore did not mean that the country could make its own foreign policy.

Bảo Đại became emperor in 1926, went back to school in France and returned to govern in 1932. His 1933 reforms changed the ministry personnel and court etiquette, including requirements to kneel before him. Even royal manners could change while the wider balance of colonial power remained unequal.

In 1930, communist-led uprisings in Nghệ An and Hà Tĩnh challenged colonial authority. That December, activists and Quốc Học students in Huế protested French airborne and ground attacks on the breakaway districts. Police arrested participants, sending some to the island prison of Côn Đảo. Classrooms and political struggle could be connected in very direct, dangerous ways.

Phú Bài’s airstrip opened in 1924. Villagers kept its ground clear and maintained sheds; by 1931 it still lacked fuel, spare parts and radio navigation. A telephone installed in 1936 let caretakers report the weather each morning. Early flying depended on people looking up at the sky, then making a call.

sections.title: Families, learning, food and practical knowledge

items.text: Đạm Phương treated education within families, and the learning of women and children, as ways to change society. In 1926 she established a vocational educational organization in Huế. She also supported the city’s student protests in 1927. Her work joined household concerns to public life, rather than leaving women’s learning confined to private rooms.

The foundation ceremony for Huế’s Đồng Khánh girls’ school in 1917 included a metal box holding nine Khải Định coins and two handwritten French records. It was a time capsule under a school. A provincial historical photograph collection also shows pre-1945 pupils on outings around the Perfume River and royal tombs, evidence that learning could include excursions as well as classroom lessons.

Huế’s Tiếng Dân printing house published women’s practical books alongside political and historical works. Volumes issued in 1928 and 1931 included instructions for foods such as sour shrimp, grilled nem and chicken salad. The contributors included Trần Thị Như Mân and other women. Cooking knowledge could travel in a printed book as well as through a family kitchen.

A 1927 book from the same press addressed household medicine and emergency aid. Its author, Hoàng Mộng Lương, was a medical officer. The surviving publication record shows readers seeking practical medical knowledge in Vietnamese. It does not tell us how many families owned the book or establish that its old remedies were effective.

Try reading a useful 1929 title: “Phép nuôi gà”, meaning “Methods of raising chickens”. Nguyễn Trọng Trử’s 68-page handbook was printed by Tiếng Dân in Huế. The National Library of France preserves copies and transcribes the title in its catalogue. The sample uses Vietnamese quốc ngữ, a Latin-based script with tone marks; the letters here are modern type reproducing the catalogued title. Chickens, too, had a place on the bookshelf.

sections.title: Water, health, work and surviving objects

items.text: Huế’s waterworks, founded in 1909, pumped from the Perfume River at Vạn Niên and settled and filtered the water at Quảng Tế hill. Early supply mainly served offices, French residents, some Vietnamese officials and wealthy families. Expansion in 1925 and 1926 increased capacity. Pipes were a significant public-health development, but this unequal service cannot be taken as evidence that every home had running water or a flush toilet.

An official 1930 statistical table counted 9,339 patients consulting Huế’s eye clinic and 32,472 consultations. The difference matters: a person could need more than one visit. Such records make a hospital’s work visible, while leaving unanswered how many people outside the clinic could obtain care or how well treatment worked.

Memorials preserved in the imperial archives show officials working out labor protections in 1938 under a law issued in November 1937. One concerned dangerous jobs for women and children; another concerned mine workers. The documents passed through both the court and French resident. They reveal negotiations over work and safety, while the existence of a rule alone cannot prove that employers followed it.

Huế’s Khải Định Museum was founded in 1923, making older court objects part of a public collection. Its 2023 centenary exhibition displayed seals, swords, ceramics and precious-metal books used for official and ceremonial records. A book could literally have metal pages. These surviving objects help historians reconstruct court craft and authority; the modern exhibition is not a complete inventory of what visitors saw in 1923.

A tiny copper-alloy coin in the British Museum belongs to Bảo Đại’s reign, 1926 to 1945. It measures 18 millimetres across and weighs 1.27 grams. Its four-character inscription made royal writing part of a pocket-sized object. The catalogue supplies a reign-wide date, so this individual coin cannot be pinned to a particular year within the atlas’s shorter interval.

ending.text: The atlas stops this record in 1938, but neither the Nguyễn monarchy nor French domination ended then. Japan’s overthrow of French administration in 1945 brought a new, Japanese-backed political arrangement. Bảo Đại formally abdicated at Huế on 30 August 1945, handing over royal symbols to representatives of the revolutionary government. These institutional ruptures did not end Vietnamese communities, languages or local traditions.
